title: Design Review: Onboarding Flow

summary.overview: Sofia presented the redesigned onboarding flow, which cuts the signup path from six screens to four and moves calendar connection to after the first value moment. Liam raised concerns about the OAuth redirect losing state, and Priya asked for analytics events on each step so drop-off can be measured. The team agreed to ship the new flow to ten percent of new signups first. Open questions remain on the copy for the permission screen and the skip behavior for the calendar step.

bullets.label: Funnel Problem
bullets.text: Only 41% of signups reach a first recorded meeting, and the calendar permission screen causes about 30% of the drop-off.

bullets.label: New Flow
bullets.text: Four screens instead of six: account creation, a sample meeting, calendar connection and a confirmation.
bullets.at: Screen three is the calendar connection

bullets.label: Sample Meeting
bullets.text: A static example meeting is shown before asking for permissions; it is a fixture, so there is no backend cost.

bullets.label: OAuth Fix
bullets.text: The OAuth redirect loses signup state; a signed state parameter fixes it in about two days.

bullets.label: Analytics
bullets.text: Priya will define events per screen view and action, with an anonymous onboarding id that survives the redirect.
bullets.at: I'll define a small set of events

bullets.label: Permission Copy
bullets.text: Two variants (benefit-first and trust-first), both stating that private events are ignored.

bullets.label: Rollout
bullets.text: Ten percent of new signups for two weeks; success is a first recorded meeting within seven days.
bullets.at: ten percent of new signups for two weeks

action_items.text: Rewrite the calendar permission screen copy and share two variants
Fix OAuth redirect so signup state survives the round trip
Define analytics events for each onboarding step and document them
Set up the ten percent rollout experiment and success metric

transcript.summary: Sofia explained that the redesign aims to show value before asking for permissions. Jordan shared that 41% of people who start signup reach a recorded meeting, and about 30% of the total drop happens at the calendar step, the single biggest leak.

points.text: Session recordings show people closing the tab at the calendar permission screen.
Principle: show people value first, then ask for permissions.

transcript: Thanks for joining. Today I want to walk through the new onboarding flow, get your feedback on feasibility, and decide what we're willing to ship in the first pass. Quick context first on why we're doing it.

Please do, and one thing I'll add is the funnel number. Right now only forty-one percent of people who start signup reach their first meeting recorded, and most of the drop happens before they connect a calendar.

Exactly. When I watched the session recordings, people hit the calendar permission screen before they understood what the product does. It's a big ask at the worst possible moment, and a lot of them just closed the tab.
Do we know how many bounce at that specific screen? I'd like to separate it from people who simply abandon the form earlier.
About thirty percent of the total drop is at the calendar step, so it is the single biggest leak. The rest is spread across the profile screens.
Is the profile drop-off something we can fix later, or does it interact with the calendar change? I want to make sure we don't redesign the same screens twice.
I looked at that. Removing the extra fields shrinks the profile step a lot, so it's part of this same change. We won't need another pass on those screens.
That's what led to the principle behind this design. Show people value first, then ask for permissions. Let me share my screen and walk you through the prototype.

transcript.summary: The new flow removes the company size and role fields, adds a sample meeting before the calendar step, and ends with a confirmation of the next meeting. Skipping the calendar step is allowed but quieter, and skippers land on a dashboard with the sample pinned.

points.text: Account creation is just email or Google sign-in; sales qualification moves to an optional prompt later.
points.at: lightweight prompt after the first week

points.text: The sample meeting shows a transcript, summary and action items so users see the outcome first.
points.at: a transcript, a summary, and action items

points.text: Skipping the calendar step is allowed through a deliberately quieter link; skippers keep the sample meeting pinned.

transcript: Screen one is account creation, email or Google sign-in, nothing else. We removed the company size question and the role dropdown. We can ask those later, once somebody is already using the product.
That removes two form fields and a validation step, so it's a nice simplification on my end too. What happens with the data we used to collect for sales qualification?
We'll ask for it in a lightweight prompt after the first week. Sales said they can live without it at signup as long as we capture it eventually.
Whatever we ask later should be skippable too. I'd hate to rebuild the same wall of fields one week in and just move the drop-off from day one to day eight.
Good point. It'll be a single optional question, not a form, and it can be dismissed permanently.

Screen two is the one I'm most excited about. Instead of an empty dashboard, we show a sample meeting with a transcript, a summary, and action items, so people can see the outcome before they invest any effort.
I love that. It also helps with the empty-state problem we've had where new users land on a blank page and have no idea what to do next.
That was a secondary goal, yes. The sample meeting also doubles as a tour. Each section has a small tooltip pointing out the summary, the action items, and the transcript so people learn the layout.
Are the tooltips part of this release? That's a library choice for me, and I'd rather not introduce something heavy for a one-time tour.
They're simple callouts. I'd say keep them minimal, static markers, not a full guided-tour library.

Screen three is the calendar connection, now with a clear explanation of what we read and what we don't. And screen four confirms the next meeting we'll join, and offers a button to invite the bot to a meeting right now.
On screen three, can people skip it? In the old flow, skipping dropped them on a blank dashboard, which I think is why we saw so many one-session users.
Yes, there's a skip link, but it's deliberately quieter than the primary button. If they skip, they get the sample meeting pinned on the dashboard along with a reminder card.

transcript.summary: Liam raised that the calendar OAuth redirect drops signup state if users switch tabs or the session cookie expires, which hurts exactly the people who reached the calendar step. He proposed a signed state parameter (about two days). The sample meeting will be a static fixture, and Priya asked for analytics events on every step.

points.text: OAuth state loss affects a small share of users, but the ones who got furthest.
points.at: it hurts more than the raw number

points.text: The sample meeting is served from the frontend bundle with the same components as a real meeting.
points.at: serve it from the frontend bundle

points.text: Only signup started and completed are tracked today, so finding the calendar leak needed session recordings.
points.at: which is why it took us watching recordings

transcript: Now the technical concern I mentioned in the doc. The calendar connection uses an OAuth redirect, and when users come back from the provider, our current signup state is lost if they started in a different tab or the session cookie expired.
I've seen that bug in the logs. It affects a small percentage of people, but those are exactly the ones who made it all the way to the calendar step, so it hurts more than the raw number suggests.
My fix is to pass a signed state parameter through the redirect that includes the onboarding step, and restore it on return. I think it's about two days of work including tests.
That sounds worth doing regardless of the redesign. Let's include it in the same release so we don't ship a prettier flow on top of a known leak.
Quick question about the sample meeting. Is that a real recording or a static mock? I'd prefer it not hit the processing pipeline for every single signup.
It's static content, a fixture. The idea is it's identical for everyone and loads instantly, so there's no backend cost.
Good, I can serve it from the frontend bundle and read it with the same components as a real meeting. That keeps it consistent and means it's easy to refresh the content later.
One thing to double check, the sample meeting should be clearly labeled as an example. I don't want support tickets from people asking why their first meeting has people they've never met in it.
Yes, there's a persistent Sample banner and the title says Example meeting. Once they record a real one, the sample can be dismissed.
Last thing on feasibility, we need analytics events at every step. Right now we only track signup started and signup completed, which is why it took us watching recordings to find the calendar leak.
I'll define a small set of events, one per screen view and one per primary action, and write them up so the engineering and data sides agree on the names.
Please include a stable session identifier in each event. Otherwise stitching a funnel together across the OAuth redirect will be painful.
Good call, I'll include an anonymous onboarding id that survives the redirect, and Liam can store it in the signed state parameter.

transcript.summary: The permission screen copy sounds invasive, so Sofia will draft two variants: one benefit-first (we'll join your meetings so you never forget to record) and one trust-first. The team will state that private events are ignored and test the structure before the copy.

points.text: Say what is not read: private events are ignored.
Run the new flow against the old one first, then optimize copy.

transcript: Let's talk about the permission screen copy, because I'm not happy with it yet. Right now it says we need access to your calendar, which sounds invasive.
Agreed. I'd focus on the benefit, something like we'll join your meetings automatically so you never forget to record. And then in smaller text, we only read event titles, times, and links.
It's also worth noting what we don't do. People worry that we read their private events. If we say private events are ignored, I think that would help a lot.
That's a great addition. Let me draft two variants, one benefit-first and one trust-first, and we can run them against each other if the experiment infrastructure allows it.
It does. We can split variants within the same rollout, but I'd keep the first test simple. One change at a time makes the results easier to read.
Good point. Let's put the new flow against the old one first, and then optimize copy once we know the structure is working.
And mobile? About a third of signups come from phones. Does the flow hold up on a small screen, especially the sample meeting?
I designed mobile first for screens one, three and four. The sample meeting collapses into tabs for summary, actions, and transcript. I'll share those frames after the call.

transcript.summary: The team agreed to a ten percent rollout of new signups for two weeks, with the share who record a first meeting within seven days as the success metric and a guardrail if completion falls by more than three points. Frontend work is about a week plus two days for the OAuth fix.

points.text: Guardrail: stop the experiment if signup completion drops by more than three points.
points.at: drops by more than three points

points.text: Final assets and copy are due Wednesday, with the build ready by the end of next week.
points.at: I'll have the assets and the final copy by Wednesday

points.text: Jordan owns experiment setup, the flag and the metrics.

transcript: So how do we roll this out? I'd propose ten percent of new signups for two weeks, and the success metric is the percentage who record their first meeting within seven days.
I'd add a guardrail metric too. If the signup completion rate drops by more than three points, we stop the experiment and investigate.
Yes, I'll write that into the experiment plan. I'll own the setup and make sure the flag and the metrics are in place before we start.
Timeline wise, the screens are about a week of frontend work, plus two days for the OAuth fix. If Sofia has the final assets by Wednesday, I can have it ready by the end of next week.
I'll have the assets and the final copy by Wednesday, with the permission screen being the only open piece.
From the backend side I don't see any blockers. I'll just need the event names from Priya so the analytics endpoint accepts them.
Great. To summarize, we're going with the four-screen flow, we're fixing the OAuth state issue, and we run it as a ten percent experiment. Thanks, Sofia, this is a big improvement.
Thanks all. I'll post the updated prototype link in the channel after the call.
